Tracing Flight: Exile, Migration and Asylum: This introductory course examines how forced migration has been portrayed and defined in German-language literature, film, and political thought from the Thirty Years’ War through the Second World War to the present-day. We will read the works of Germanophone exile writers and political thinkers, German-Turkish authors, and contemporary texts and films relating to the more recently termed European refugee “crisis” in English translation. In view of policy responses to large-scale migration and waning support for refugees in Europe coinciding with the rise of far-right political parties, this course asks how the terms "exile," "migrant," and "refugee" have been culturally and legally defined, how they are handled in public discourse, and whether these categories are distinct or overlapping. This course aims to offer students a comparative framework for analyzing forced migration across historical periods and culminates in independent research projects. No prerequisites or prior knowledge necessary; taught IN ENGLISH.

sections.note: This course will look at what it means to be ‘humorous’ (including satire & irony) giving examples in German-language popular culture, including stories, cinema, television, stand-up, music, and YouTube. In particular, the course will analyze how humor is expressed within German popular culture in order to comment on society in a critical way. To put this another way, we will use German-language cultural works to explore the main question: What is the function of German popular humor? We will consider several related sub-questions: Is humor a “low form” of cultural representation? Is humor essentially derived from distain of or condescension toward others? the object of the joke? the BUTT of the joke, in English? This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for Western Literature and the Arts or Western Cultural Studies.

GER 205: Germany and Europe: Europe in Trouble? This course reads Europe’s postwar history as a series of crises, illuminating broader European dynamics that have shaped Europe as we know it today. It may seem like Europe is in trouble all the time, and yet the European Union has proven to be more relevant and resilient than ever. The central theme concerns Europe’s "struggle for identity" in relation to other global powers that underlies many of the controversies surrounding Europe’s global role today. Particular attention will be paid to debates on migration, religion, language, and the long-term effects of World War II. Course material includes Tony Judt’s Postwar: A History of Europe since 1945, in-class screenings of several films, and Milan Kundera’s novel The Unbearable Lightness of Being. Satisfies the Gen Ed requirements for "Historical and Philosophical Perspectives" and "Western/Comparative Cultures". No prerequisites or prior knowledge necessary; taught IN ENGLISH.GER 205:

German 211 and German 212 are sequenced, advanced German language courses that aim to help students develop greater ease and sophistication in their oral and written expression in German. German 211 covers past and contemporary issues of the German-speaking world, including: travel and leisure; literature, art, and music; environmental issues and politics; and migration and multiculturalism. Students will also read Thomas Brussig's 1999 novel Am kürzeren Ende der Sonnenallee to develop interpretative skills in German and deepened cultural knowledge of Germany's past, specifically East Germany during the 1970's. Day1Access course materials cost $62.88. For more information see https://go.illinois.edu/Day1Access.

German 211 and German 212 are sequenced, advanced German language courses that aim to help students develop greater ease and sophistication in their oral and written expression in German. German 212 covers issues in modern history and contemporary German society through focus on literature, art and film. Students will also read a full-length novel (Bernhard Schlink's Der Vorleser) to develop interpretative skills in German and deepened cultural knowledge of Germany's past. Through the 211-212 course sequence, students will become prepared for advanced coursework in German literature and culture, as well as study in a German-speaking country. GER 251 / ENGL 266 / CWL 254 The Grimms’ Fairy Tales in Context Get ready to experience tales you thought you knew and tales you never knew. We read substantial parts of the Grimms' 19th-century collections and some of their French and Italian predecessors, and we consider other storytelling forms, film, and illustration. All the while, we investigate how power, gender, race, class, and ecological issues play out in these surprisingly dense, meaningful, and very old stories. Why do we continue to tell and to know these tales? Why do certain stories recur again and again, in Western and other cultures? The power of narrative is at the center of our lives, and of these tales, and by the end of the semester we will understand this power much better. This course fulfills General Education requirements in Literature and the Arts and in Western and Comparative Culture.

This course surveys the range of literary, theoretical, and audiovisual forms through which the Holocaust has been represented since 1945, from narrative testimony, critical essays and poetry to graphic novels and film. Students will develop insight into the fundamental concerns and challenges emerging from the aftermath of the Shoah through close readings of works by figures such as Primo Levi, Hannah Arendt, Ruth Klüger, Paul Celan, and Art Spiegelman, and engage with relevant philosophical debates thematized in depictions of German cultural memory. We will consider questions surrounding the possibility of witnessing, the role of secondhand memory, and the ethics and representational modes of Holocaust memorialization. By the end of this course, students will be able to closely read literary and filmic texts, assess the stakes of Holocaust representation, and formulate informed arguments about the politics of memory.

sections.note: Exploration of German culture, history, and literature from the late eighteenth century (Enlightenment) to the present. Our texts engage with reason and madness, love and sexuality, technology and modernization, justice and guilt, community and identity. To better understand the historical and cultural contexts in which these texts were produced, we will draw on paintings, photography, philosophy, social and political history, and film.

Language & Minorities in Europe. Credit: 3 or 4 hours. Survey of regional and immigrant minority language use, policies, and planning across Europe. Focus on political and social issues, such as language regimes, education, loss, and maintenance. Two immigrant languages, Turkish and Arabic/Berber, and four indigenous language families: Balto-Slavic with Estonian, Celtic, Romance with Basque, and Slavic with Hungarian. Taught in English. Same as GER 418, ITAL 418, LING 418, PS 418, SLAV 418, SPAN 418, and EURO 418. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.

Topic: Die deutsche Sprache im europäischen Kontext. This course examines German as a European language. Topics include the linguistic history of German, German as a standard/official/institutional language, German as a minority language, German linguistic enclaves, and German as a second/foreign language. The course also explores German language contact, variation, and change. The course is taught in German; students who have not taken GER 212 or do not have equivalent language proficiency should obtain instructor consent to enroll.

sections.note: Antifascist, humanist, witness: Rereading Christa Wolf across the 20th/21st century: In this seminar we examine the work of East German writer Christa Wolf as a “poetic lens” for understanding how to live, create, write, and survive inside systems that appear to have established their normalcy. Wolf (1929–2011) lived through nearly every rupture of the European twentieth century: a childhood inside the Third Reich, the founding of an antifascist socialist state, decades under Stasi surveillance, and a reunification met, in turn, with Western triumphalism and her own public skepticism. This seminar offers a rare, sustained immersion in a single body of work, tracing Wolf’s fiction and essays from Geteilter Himmel through Kassandra and Stadt der Engel as a continuous inquiry into what it means to act, remember, and write from inside a radically shifting world, while clinging to and recomposing humanist visions. We follow Wolf’s writing as it moves from a state that declared its own innocence of fascism, through Romantic precedents of illness, grief, and withdrawal, into the fallout of ecological catastrophe, and finally to Greek myth as a form able to name what realism under socialism elides. Throughout, we track her concept of subjective authenticity—a writing that refuses false objectivity while insisting a situated, fallible voice still carries truth. Theoretical interlocutors (Arendt, Lear, Butler, among others) enter our discussions as company Wolf’s texts are already keeping. Discussions in English, readings in German (and available in English). Meets with GER 575

This course examines the language and cultures of online spaces, from multiplayer games and livestreaming communities to forums and text-based worlds. Students will explore a community firsthand, share their environments with their fellow students, and develop a research proposal based on what they discover
